pos: n. and v. (a winged insect, sent as a plague and used as a figure of small corruption; also to move on wings)
etymology: Old English fleoge, an insect, and fleogan, to move through the air. The Hebrew arob of the fourth plague is a swarm; zebub is the common fly, and gives the name Baalzebub, lord of the flies.
biblical_def: The fourth plague on Egypt: “Else, if thou wilt not let my people go, behold, I will send swarms of flies upon thee, and upon thy servants, and upon thy people, and into thy houses” (Exo 8:21); and it came — “there came a grievous swarm of flies into the house of Pharaoh, and into his servants' houses, and into all the land of Egypt: the land was corrupted by reason of the swarm of flies” (Exo 8:24). The psalmist sets it in one line of a history: “He spake, and there came divers sorts of flies, and lice in all their coasts” (Psa 105:31) — he spake, and an empire was undone by insects. Isaiah makes the fly an instrument of summons: “the LORD shall hiss for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria” (Isa 7:18), armies called like insects with a whistle. And Ecclesiastes gives the proverb that has outlived the plague: “Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour: so doth a little folly him that is in reputation for wisdom and honour” (Ecc 10:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a fly as a winged insect of various species, and to fly as to move through air by the aid of wings; also to move swiftly, or to flee.
webster_full: FLY, v.i. To move through air by the aid of wings, as fowls.
2. To move or pass with velocity or celerity.
3. To flee; to run away; to attempt to escape.
FLY, n. A winged insect of numerous species. Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour. Eccl. x.
scriptures: Exo 8:21

Else, if thou wilt not let my people go, behold, I will send swarms of flies upon thee, and upon thy servants, and upon thy people, and into thy houses: and the houses of the Egyptians shall be full of swarms of flies, and also the ground whereon they are.
Exo 8:24

And the LORD did so; and there came a grievous swarm of flies into the house of Pharaoh, and into his servants' houses, and into all the land of Egypt: the land was corrupted by reason of the swarm of flies.
Ecc 10:1
Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour: so doth a little folly him that is in reputation for wisdom and honour.
Isa 7:18
And it shall come to pass in that day, that the LORD shall hiss for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria.
corruption_summary: A long-built reputation is thought to absorb a small folly, and Ecclesiastes says the small folly is exactly what ruins the whole jar.
corruption_paragraphs: The Preacher's figure is a pot of costly ointment — the apothecary's work, compounded with care and worth a great deal — and two dead flies in it. The ointment is not diluted; it is spoiled, and what comes out of the jar now is a stinking savour. He then names the application without softening it: so doth a little folly him that is in reputation for wisdom and honour. The modern instinct is to weigh a man's failures against his contribution and conclude that the ledger still favours him, and there is a place for that charity; Scripture does not erase David for Bathsheba or Peter for the courtyard. But the proverb is about savour rather than accounting. A little folly in a man of standing changes what people smell when the jar is opened, and no quantity of former excellence puts the flies back out.

The plague half of the word carries a different warning. Egypt's gods included flies and beetles, and Ekron worshipped Baalzebub, the lord of the flies, whose name the Jews later used for the prince of the devils. God's judgment on Egypt came through the creatures Egypt revered — the Nile turned, the frogs, the flies, the cattle, the sun darkened — so that each plague dismantled a deity. And Psalm 105 gives the whole account in three words: he spake. Isaiah's image extends it to nations: the LORD hisses, as a beekeeper whistles his swarm, and Egypt and Assyria come. Empires that never heard of Him move at a signal. That is the doctrine of providence over the nations, and it is why the church may be sober about world events without being frightened by them.
roots_summary: Hebrew arob (H6157), a swarm of flies, of the fourth plague; zebub (H2070), a fly, and the element in Baalzebub; Greek Beelzeboul (G954), the prince of the devils.
roots_lines: Hebrew arob (H6157) — a mixture, a swarm; swarms of flies upon Pharaoh and his houses; Exodus 8:21.
Hebrew zebub (H2070) — a fly; dead flies in the apothecary's ointment; Ecclesiastes 10:1.
Hebrew Baal zebub — lord of the fly; the god of Ekron whom Ahaziah consulted; 2 Kings 1:2.
Hebrew sharaq (H8319) — to hiss, to whistle; the LORD shall hiss for the fly; Isaiah 7:18.
Greek Beelzeboul (G954) — Beelzebub, the prince of the devils in the Gospels; Matthew 12:24.
usage: “The land was corrupted by reason of the swarm of flies” — an empire undone by insects.
“He spake, and there came divers sorts of flies” — the whole account in three words.
“Dead flies cause the ointment… to send forth a stinking savour” — a little folly in a man of reputation.

pos: n. (a small biting insect; David's own figure for himself when a king was hunting him)
etymology: Old English fleah. The Hebrew parosh occurs twice, both times in David's mouth, and both times as a measure of how little he was worth pursuing.
biblical_def: David used the word twice, in the two scenes where he had Saul in his power and refused him. In the cave at Engedi, after cutting the skirt of Saul's robe and letting him go, he called after him: “After whom is the king of Israel come out? after whom dost thou pursue? after a dead dog, after a flea” (1Sa 24:14). And in the wilderness of Ziph, after taking the spear from beside Saul's head: “Now therefore, let not my blood fall to the earth before the face of the LORD: for the king of Israel is come out to seek a flea, as when one doth hunt a partridge in the mountains” (1Sa 26:20). The picture is a king with three thousand chosen men hunting a single insect through the hills. David's point is not merely self-abasement; it is the absurdity of the whole campaign, and the waste of a kingdom's strength on a private jealousy. He is also, in both scenes, refusing to lift his hand against the LORD's anointed — a man with a throne promised him, waiting for God to give it rather than taking it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a flea as an insect of the genus Pulex, remarkable for its agility in leaping, and troublesome by its bite.
webster_full: FLEA, n. [Sax. flea; from the root of flee, to spring.] An insect of the genus Pulex.
The flea has a compressed body, and is remarkable for its agility in leaping.
After whom dost thou pursue? after a dead dog, after a flea. 1 Sam. xxiv.
FLEA, v.t. To clean from fleas.
scriptures: After whom is the king of Israel come out? after whom dost thou pursue? after a dead dog, after a flea.
Now therefore, let not my blood fall to the earth before the face of the LORD: for the king of Israel is come out to seek a flea, as when one doth hunt a partridge in the mountains.
There be four things which are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise:
The locusts have no king, yet go they forth all of them by bands;
corruption_summary: Self-deprecation is now a social manner rather than a judgment about oneself, while David's flea is a statement made under pressure by a man who could have taken the throne that night.
corruption_paragraphs: It is easy to hear after a dead dog, after a flea as the polite modesty of a courtier, and to miss where David was standing when he said it. He had just come out of a cave holding a piece of Saul's robe; in the other scene he was holding Saul's own spear, taken from beside the king's head while the whole camp slept. Abishai had offered to pin Saul to the earth with one stroke and asked no second permission. David's refusal — who can stretch forth his hand against the LORD's anointed, and be guiltless? — is the context of the flea. A man who genuinely holds himself small is not the man who has nothing; he is the man who has the opportunity and does not take it. Modern self-deprecation costs nothing because it is spoken by people with no spear in their hand.

The second thing worth naming is what David refuses to do with a promise. He had been anointed by Samuel years before; the kingdom was pledged to him by God; Saul was demonstrably rejected. Every argument for seizing the moment was available, and Abishai even framed it as providence — God hath delivered thine enemy into thine hand this day. David answers that the LORD shall smite him, or his day shall come to die, or he shall descend into battle and perish; but not by my hand. That is one of the clearest tests in Scripture of the difference between believing a promise and forcing it. Providence supplying an opportunity is not the same as God commanding an act, and a Christian who has learned to tell those two apart has learned something most men never do.
roots_summary: Hebrew parosh (H6550), a flea; used only in David's two speeches to Saul; with meshiach YHWH, the LORD's anointed, the reason for his restraint.
roots_lines: Hebrew parosh (H6550) — a flea; after a dead dog, after a flea; 1 Samuel 24:14, 1 Samuel 26:20.
Hebrew keleb meth — a dead dog; the companion figure of worthlessness; 1 Samuel 24:14.
Hebrew mashiach (H4899) — anointed; the title David would not lift his hand against; 1 Samuel 24:6.
Hebrew qore (H7124) — a partridge; the bird hunted in the hills, David's second figure; 1 Samuel 26:20.
Hebrew radaph (H7291) — to pursue; after whom dost thou pursue; 1 Samuel 24:14.
usage: “After a dead dog, after a flea” — said with the king's robe in his hand.
“The king of Israel is come out to seek a flea” — three thousand men after one insect.
“Let not my blood fall to the earth before the face of the LORD” — an appeal, not a threat.

pos: n. (a large stinging wasp; the means by which God says He drove out the nations before Israel)
etymology: Old English hyrnet, akin to horn. The Hebrew tsirah is a hornet or wasp, and it appears three times, always of God's own agency in the conquest.
biblical_def: The promise is given before the crossing: “And I will send hornets before thee, which shall drive out the Hivite, the Canaanite, and the Hittite, from before thee” (Exo 23:28), and repeated: “Moreover the LORD thy God will send the hornet among them, until they that are left, and hide themselves from thee, be destroyed” (Deu 7:20). Joshua, at the end of his life, tells the nation it happened: “And I sent the hornet before you, which drave them out from before you, even the two kings of the Amorites; but not with thy sword, nor with thy bow” (Jos 24:12). That closing clause is the doctrine of the whole conquest in six words. Israel fought real battles with real weapons, and God says the land was not taken by them. Whether the hornets were literal insects or a figure for the terror and confusion God sent ahead of the armies, the point of the verse is unchanged and is stated explicitly: not with thy sword, nor with thy bow. The victory belonged to the LORD, and the men who swung the swords are told so to their faces.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a hornet as a large strong species of wasp, of a dark brown color, whose sting is severe and irritating.
webster_full: HORNET, n. [Sax. hyrnet.] A large strong insect of the wasp kind, of a dark brown color.
The sting of the hornet is severe, and the insect is fierce and dangerous.
I will send hornets before thee. Ex. xxiii.
The hornet builds a nest of a substance resembling paper.
scriptures: And I will send hornets before thee, which shall drive out the Hivite, the Canaanite, and the Hittite, from before thee.
Deu 7:20
Moreover the LORD thy God will send the hornet among them, until they that are left, and hide themselves from thee, be destroyed.
And I sent the hornet before you, which drave them out from before you, even the two kings of the Amorites; but not with thy sword, nor with thy bow.
Isa 7:18
And it shall come to pass in that day, that the LORD shall hiss for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria.
corruption_summary: The conquest is discussed only as a moral problem about violence, while Joshua 24:12 insists the decisive agency was not Israel's at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Every generation asks about the conquest of Canaan, and the question deserves an answer rather than a shrug. Scripture gives several. The judgment was announced four hundred years in advance and delayed because the iniquity of the Amorites was not yet full. It was judicial, not ethnic: Rahab of Jericho and the Gibeonites were spared, and Israel herself was warned that the land would spew her out for the same sins. And it was limited — a specific commission against specific nations at a specific time, never a general licence, which is why the New Testament church is given no sword at all and told that the weapons of our warfare are not carnal. What Joshua 24:12 adds is the part almost never quoted: God claims the driving out as His own act and denies the sword and bow their credit, which removes the one thing a conquering people always wants, which is glory.

The hornet is worth thinking about as a means. It is not an angel with a flaming sword; it is an insect, or the terror an insect stands for. God's deliverances in Scripture come by small and unglamorous instruments — a stammering shepherd, a boy's sling, a jawbone, a widow's meal barrel, a little maid in Naaman's house, five loaves. Paul draws the rule: God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty, that no flesh should glory in his presence. Israel entered the land behind hornets, and afterwards had nothing to boast of but the promise of God. A church that wants to see God work should notice what He has generally used, and stop despising the smallness of what is at hand.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsirah (H6880), a hornet or wasp; used three times, always of God's sending; with garash (H1644), to drive out, and yarash (H3423), to dispossess.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsirah (H6880) — a hornet; I will send hornets before thee; Exodus 23:28, Deuteronomy 7:20, Joshua 24:12.
Hebrew garash (H1644) — to drive out, to expel; which shall drive out the Hivite, the Canaanite, and the Hittite; Exodus 23:28.
Hebrew yarash (H3423) — to possess by dispossessing; the standing verb of the conquest; Deuteronomy 7:1.
Hebrew chereb (H2719) — a sword; not with thy sword, nor with thy bow; Joshua 24:12.
Hebrew emah (H367) — terror, dread; I will send my fear before thee; Exodus 23:27.
usage: “I will send hornets before thee” — the promise, given before the crossing.
“Until they that are left, and hide themselves from thee, be destroyed” — a judgment long announced.
“Not with thy sword, nor with thy bow” — the conquest's doctrine in six words.

pos: n. (a burrowing creature of the unclean list; and, with the bat, what men will throw their idols to in the day of the LORD)
etymology: Middle English molle, a burrower, related to mould, the earth. The Hebrew tinshemeth at Leviticus 11:30 is an unidentified creeping thing; chapharperah at Isaiah 2:20 is literally a digger, from the verb to dig.
biblical_def: The mole closes the list of creeping things forbidden to Israel: “And the ferret, and the chameleon, and the lizard, and the snail, and the mole” (Lev 11:30), the last of eight named in two verses, all classed with the weasel, the mouse and the tortoise as “unclean unto you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth” (Lev 11:29). The law adds the practical consequence: “These are unclean to you among all that creep: whosoever doth touch them, when they be dead, shall be unclean until the even” (Lev 11:31). Isaiah gives the creature its great moment: “In that day a man shall cast his idols of silver, and his idols of gold, which they made each one for himself to worship, to the moles and to the bats” (Isa 2:20). When the terror of the LORD comes, men will fling the gods they commissioned into the dark holes where blind diggers live — not selling them, not repenting of them, simply throwing them away in a panic and going into the clefts of the rocks.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the mole as a small animal of the genus Talpa, that burrows in the earth and throws up little hillocks; almost blind, with very small eyes.
webster_full: MOLE, n. [Sax. moldwarp, mold-warp, earth-caster.] A small animal of the genus Talpa, that burrows in the earth.
The eyes are very small, and covered with a membrane, so that the animal is nearly blind.
A man shall cast his idols… to the moles and to the bats. Isa. ii.
MOLE, n. A spot or mark on the human body.
scriptures: And the ferret, and the chameleon, and the lizard, and the snail, and the mole.
These also shall be unclean unto you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth; the weasel, and the mouse, and the tortoise after his kind,
Isa 2:20
In that day a man shall cast his idols of silver, and his idols of gold, which they made each one for himself to worship, to the moles and to the bats;

For I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy: neither shall ye defile yourselves with any manner of creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.
corruption_summary: Idolatry is imagined as belief in a statue, though Isaiah 2:20 shows men who made their gods themselves, knew it, and kept them until the day they were terrified.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah's clause is exact and it destroys the comfortable idea that idolaters were merely mistaken about metallurgy. The idols are of silver and of gold, and they were made each one for himself to worship. The man commissioned his god, paid for it, knew where the metal came from, and worshipped it anyway. That is not ignorance; it is the human heart doing what Romans says it does, changing the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image. And the day of reckoning does not produce repentance in Isaiah's picture — it produces panic. The idols go into the mole-holes because their owners are running for the caves, and the same chapter says the loftiness of man shall be bowed down, and the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day.

The mole is a fitting recipient for two reasons the passage means us to feel. It is blind, and it lives underground. The gods men made for themselves end in the dark, held by something that cannot see them, which is exactly what Psalm 115 says of the idols and their makers: eyes have they, but they see not; they that make them are like unto them; so is every one that trusteth in them. And the creature is unclean by the law — the last named in a list of things Israel must not so much as touch when dead. So the idol of silver, the most valuable object in a man's house, is thrown to the least clean and least seeing thing in the land. Isaiah's scorn is not cruelty; it is the mercy of showing a man now what his treasure will be worth then.
roots_summary: Hebrew tinshemeth (H8580), an unclean creeping thing, rendered mole at Leviticus 11:30; chapharperah (H2661), a digger or mole, at Isaiah 2:20; with elil (H457), an idol, a thing of nought.
roots_lines: Hebrew tinshemeth (H8580) — rendered mole among the creeping things; Leviticus 11:30.
Hebrew chapharperah (H2661) — a digger, a mole; from chaphar, to dig; Isaiah 2:20.
Hebrew atalleph (H5847) — a bat; named with the mole as the recipient of cast-off idols; Isaiah 2:20.
Hebrew elil (H457) — a thing of nought, an idol; the standing contemptuous word; Psalm 96:5.
Hebrew sheqets (H8263) — an abomination, a detestable thing; the classification of the creeping things; Leviticus 11:41.
usage: “And the ferret, and the chameleon… and the mole” — last of the unclean creepers.
“Which they made each one for himself to worship” — idolatry with full knowledge.
“To the moles and to the bats” — silver gods thrown to a blind digger.

pos: n. (a creeping thing of the unclean list; probably a gecko or a small burrowing animal)
etymology: Old French furet, from Latin fur, a thief — the little thief. The Hebrew anaqah is from a root meaning to cry out or groan, so the creature is named for a sound rather than a shape; many identify it with the gecko.
biblical_def: The word occurs once, first in the list of Leviticus 11:30: “And the ferret, and the chameleon, and the lizard, and the snail, and the mole.” It belongs with the seven other creatures of verses twenty-nine and thirty, all of them “unclean unto you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth” (Lev 11:29). The rule attached is not about eating only: “whosoever doth touch them, when they be dead, shall be unclean until the even” (Lev 11:31). Anyone who has kept a house in a hot country knows why the list is full of the creatures that get into houses. And the chapter closes with the reason for the whole catalogue, which is not hygiene and not zoology: “For I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy” (Lev 11:44). Peter quotes that verse to Christians who eat what they like, which is the clearest statement in the New Testament of what these chapters were always for.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the ferret as an animal of the weasel kind, red-eyed and used to drive rabbits from their burrows; and, as a verb, to drive out of a lurking place.
webster_full: FERRET, n. [Fr. furet; L. fur, a thief.] An animal of the genus Mustela, or weasel kind, with red eyes.
It is used in driving rabbits out of their holes.
The ferret, and the chameleon, and the lizard. Lev. xi.
FERRET, v.t. To drive out of a lurking place, as a ferret does a rabbit.
scriptures: And the ferret, and the chameleon, and the lizard, and the snail, and the mole.
These are unclean to you among all that creep: whosoever doth touch them, when they be dead, shall be unclean until the even.

For I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy: neither shall ye defile yourselves with any manner of creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.
These also shall be unclean unto you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth; the weasel, and the mouse, and the tortoise after his kind,
corruption_summary: The dietary law is explained as ancient public health, which is to answer a question Leviticus 11:44 has already answered in the opposite terms.
corruption_paragraphs: The hygienic theory of the clean and unclean laws is popular in both directions — sceptics use it to make the law merely primitive medicine, and defenders use it to make the Bible scientifically advanced. Leviticus itself gives a different reason, and gives it as the conclusion of the whole chapter: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy. The distinctions were a daily, tactile discipline in separation, worked into what a family could put on the table, so that a nation could not eat a meal without being reminded that it belonged to God and was not like the peoples around it. That is a theological purpose, not a medical one, and it explains features no hygiene theory can — why touching a dead one defiles until evening, why the same chapter regulates ovens and vessels, and why the whole system is later declared fulfilled rather than merely outgrown.

That last point is where Christians must be careful in both directions. The Lord Jesus declared all meats clean, Peter was told on the housetop not to call common what God had cleansed, and Paul writes that the kingdom of God is not meat and drink. The ceremonial distinctions are fulfilled in Christ and are not binding on the church; a believer who reimposes them has, Colossians says, submitted to ordinances after the commandments and doctrines of men. But the purpose behind them is not abolished, because Peter quotes Leviticus 11:44 to Gentile churches: be ye holy; for I am holy. The separation moved from the plate to the life. What was once taught by a list of creatures is now taught by conduct, speech, and the ordering of a household — and the God who required it has not changed.
roots_summary: Hebrew anaqah (H604), rendered ferret; from a root meaning to groan or cry out; with sheqets (H8263), a detestable thing, and qadash (H6942), to sanctify.
roots_lines: Hebrew anaqah (H604) — rendered ferret; from anaq, to cry out, so named from its sound; Leviticus 11:30.
Hebrew remes (H7431) — creeping things; the class to which the eight belong; Leviticus 11:29.
Hebrew tame (H2931) — unclean; the verdict on the whole list; Leviticus 11:31.
Hebrew qadash (H6942) — to sanctify, to set apart; ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves; Leviticus 11:44.
Greek hagios (G40) — holy; be ye holy; for I am holy, quoted to the churches; 1 Peter 1:16.
usage: “And the ferret, and the chameleon, and the lizard” — the creatures that get into houses.
“Whosoever doth touch them, when they be dead, shall be unclean until the even” — a daily discipline.
“Ye shall be holy; for I am holy” — the stated reason for the whole chapter.

pos: n. (a creeping thing of the unclean list; the lizard proverbial for changing its colour)
etymology: Greek chamaileon, ground-lion, from chamai, on the ground, and leon, a lion. The Hebrew koach means strength, so the creature is named in Hebrew for its power and in Greek for its lowliness.
biblical_def: It stands second in the list: “And the ferret, and the chameleon, and the lizard, and the snail, and the mole” (Lev 11:30), among the eight creatures declared “unclean unto you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth” (Lev 11:29). Scripture says nothing about its changing colour; the association is ours and the ancients'. But the law does say something the trait makes vivid. Israel was to be a people whose distinctness was visible and constant, and the whole chapter is a discipline against blending in: “For I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy” (Lev 11:44). And the touching rule is what makes it daily: “whosoever doth touch them, when they be dead, shall be unclean until the even” (Lev 11:31). A nation that must ask what it may touch is a nation continually reminded whose it is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the chameleon as an animal of the lizard kind, remarkable for its power of changing colour; and figuratively, one who changes opinions to suit the company.
webster_full: CHAMELEON, n. [Gr. a ground lion.] An animal of the genus Lacerta, or lizard.
It has the faculty of changing its color, which was formerly ascribed to its taking the color of surrounding objects.
The ferret, and the chameleon, and the lizard. Lev. xi.
Figuratively, a person who changes his opinions or manners to please others.
scriptures: And the ferret, and the chameleon, and the lizard, and the snail, and the mole.

For I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy: neither shall ye defile yourselves with any manner of creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.
These are unclean to you among all that creep: whosoever doth touch them, when they be dead, shall be unclean until the even.
These also shall be unclean unto you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth; the weasel, and the mouse, and the tortoise after his kind,
corruption_summary: Adapting to every company is now called relatability and treated as a ministry skill, while Scripture requires a distinctness that can be seen from outside.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the creature itself; the principle to recover is the difference between accommodation and colour-changing. Paul made himself all things to all men, and the sentence is often quoted to justify a ministry that takes on the tone, tastes and moral vocabulary of whatever room it is in. What Paul actually did was surrender preferences and rights — his liberty, his maintenance, his standing on ceremonial matters — and he states the fixed purpose that governed it: that I might by all means save some. He did not adjust the message, and in the same epistles he refuses to give place by subjection, no, not for an hour, where the truth of the gospel is at stake. The line is not always easy to draw in practice, but it exists, and it runs between what a man gives up and what he says.

Leviticus 11 shows why visible distinctness matters to God. He could have taught Israel holiness by doctrine alone; He taught it instead through what they ate, what they touched, what pots they used and how long a defilement lasted, so that separation was not an idea but a texture. The New Testament changes the means and keeps the end: Christians are told not to be conformed to this world, to come out from among them and be separate, and to have their conversation honest among the Gentiles. A church that is indistinguishable from its surroundings in speech, appetite, marriage and money has not become relatable; it has changed colour. And the change is rarely decided; like the creature, it happens by resting a long time against the same background.
roots_summary: Hebrew koach (H3581) as a creature name, rendered chameleon; with letaah (H3911), the lizard beside it, and the chapter's governing verb qadash (H6942), to sanctify.
roots_lines: Hebrew koach (H3581) — rendered chameleon in the list; the same consonants as the common word for strength; Leviticus 11:30.
Hebrew letaah (H3911) — a lizard; named next to it; Leviticus 11:30.
Hebrew badal (H914) — to divide, to separate; that ye may put difference between holy and unholy; Leviticus 10:10.
Hebrew qadash (H6942) — to sanctify, to set apart as holy; Leviticus 11:44.
Greek suschematizo (G4964) — to conform to a pattern; be not conformed to this world; Romans 12:2.
usage: “The ferret, and the chameleon, and the lizard” — second in the unclean list.
“Ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves” — separation taught by texture, not by lecture.

pos: n. (a small four-footed reptile; third in the list of unclean creeping things)
etymology: Old French lesarde, from Latin lacertus. The Hebrew letaah denotes a lizard of some common kind; the word occurs once in Scripture.
biblical_def: “And the ferret, and the chameleon, and the lizard, and the snail, and the mole” (Lev 11:30). The lizard belongs to the eight creatures listed in Leviticus 11:29-30 as “unclean unto you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth” (Lev 11:29), with the rule that touching one dead defiles until evening (Lev 11:31). Proverbs, in the great passage on things little and exceeding wise, describes a creature that takes hold with her hands and is in kings' palaces (Pro 30:28) — rendered spider in the Authorized Version and understood by many as a lizard, which would make the last of Agur's four small wonders a house lizard on a palace wall. Either way the lesson Agur draws is the same: “There be four things which are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise” (Pro 30:24). The unclean list and the wisdom list stand together without contradiction. A creature may be excluded from Israel's table and still be set before Israel's wise men as a teacher.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the lizard as an animal of the genus Lacerta, a four-footed reptile with a long slender body and tail, of many species and generally harmless.
webster_full: LIZARD, n. [Fr. lesarde; L. lacerta.] An animal of the genus Lacerta.
The body is oblong, with four legs, and a long tapering tail.
The ferret, and the chameleon, and the lizard. Lev. xi.
Most species are harmless and are found in warm climates.
scriptures: And the ferret, and the chameleon, and the lizard, and the snail, and the mole.
There be four things which are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise:
The spider taketh hold with her hands, and is in kings' palaces.
These also shall be unclean unto you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth; the weasel, and the mouse, and the tortoise after his kind,
corruption_summary: Creation is treated as either sacred in itself or as raw material, while Scripture makes small creatures teachers without ever making them holy.
corruption_paragraphs: Agur's four little things — the ants, the conies, the locusts and the creature on the palace wall — are set before a wise man as instructors: they are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise. Job is told to ask the beasts and they shall teach thee, and the Lord Jesus said, Behold the fowls of the air, and Consider the lilies. Scripture treats the creation as a genuine source of instruction because God made it and it declares His handiwork. What it never does is make a creature sacred, which is the corruption on one side; nor does it treat the creation as mere stock for use, which is the corruption on the other. Man is given dominion and is answerable for it, and a righteous man regardeth the life of his beast.

The two lists in this entry hold both truths at once. Leviticus puts the lizard among the things Israel might not eat and might not touch dead; Proverbs puts a creature of the same sort in a king's palace as a picture of small, tenacious wisdom. Nothing in the law implies that unclean creatures are evil in themselves — God pronounced everything He made good, and the New Testament says every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving. The distinctions were appointed for Israel's separation for a season, not to divide the animal kingdom into virtue and vice. A Christian is therefore free to admire a lizard on a wall, to eat what he likes, and to remember that the reason the chapter existed was holiness.

pos: n. (a creature of the unclean list, named with the weasel and the mouse; probably a large lizard)
etymology: Old French tortue, from a late Latin word for a twisted-footed creature. The Hebrew tsab is uncertain; it may name a great lizard, and the same word elsewhere denotes a covered wagon or litter.
biblical_def: The word occurs once, opening the second of the two verses that list the unclean creepers: “These also shall be unclean unto you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth; the weasel, and the mouse, and the tortoise after his kind” (Lev 11:29), followed by the ferret, chameleon, lizard, snail and mole (Lev 11:30). The phrase after his kind is worth noticing; it recurs through the creation account and through this chapter, and it assumes fixed kinds of creature that reproduce as such. The touching rule follows: “These are unclean to you among all that creep: whosoever doth touch them, when they be dead, shall be unclean until the even” (Lev 11:31). And the whole catalogue is closed with its purpose: “ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy” (Lev 11:44). The identification of the animal is uncertain and the law's intent is not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the tortoise as an animal of the genus Testudo, covered with a shell, of both land and water kinds; the land species is the tortoise, the water the turtle.
webster_full: TORTOISE, n. tortis. [Fr. tortue; L. tortus, twisted.] An animal of the genus Testudo.
The body is covered with a shell or crust, formed of plates.
The weasel, and the mouse, and the tortoise after his kind. Lev. xi.
The land tortoise moves slowly and lives to a great age.
scriptures: These also shall be unclean unto you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth; the weasel, and the mouse, and the tortoise after his kind,
And the ferret, and the chameleon, and the lizard, and the snail, and the mole.
These are unclean to you among all that creep: whosoever doth touch them, when they be dead, shall be unclean until the even.

For I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy: neither shall ye defile yourselves with any manner of creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.
corruption_summary: Uncertainty about which animal a Hebrew word names is used to cast doubt on the text itself, when the doubt belongs to zoology and not to Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: Several creatures in Leviticus 11 cannot now be identified with confidence, and translators from the Septuagint onward have differed — tortoise, great lizard, crocodile, toad. That fact is sometimes pressed into service as an argument against the reliability of Scripture, and it proves nothing of the kind. The text has been faithfully transmitted; what has been lost is the ordinary field knowledge of a people who did not need to be told which creature tsab meant, any more than an English writer needs to define a badger. Doctrinal certainty has never rested on the identification of every species in an ancient list, and the doctrine of verbal inspiration is not a claim that every reader in every century will know exactly which lizard is meant. What God gave was given, and what is obscure is obscure to us.

The phrase after his kind is the part of the verse that matters most, and it repeats through Genesis 1 and through this chapter with the regularity of a refrain. It assumes a created order of distinct kinds that produce their own sort, and it is the same assumption behind the law's prohibitions on mixing seed, cloth and cattle. That is a claim about the world, not merely about Israel's kitchen, and it is one modern accounts of origins deny outright: on the standard account there are no fixed kinds at all, only a continuum. Scripture's doctrine of creation stands where it always has — God made the creatures after their kinds, He made man in His own image, and the difference between those two sentences is where every debate about human dignity finally rests.

“Unclean until the even” — the daily reach of the statute.

pos: n. (a creeping thing of the unclean list; and in the Psalms the figure of a wicked man melting away)
etymology: Old English snaegl, akin to snake — a creeping thing. Two Hebrew words are rendered snail: chomet in Leviticus, and shabbelul in Psalm 58, from a root suggesting moisture or slime.
biblical_def: In the law it is fourth in the list: “And the ferret, and the chameleon, and the lizard, and the snail, and the mole” (Lev 11:30), among the creeping things declared unclean (Lev 11:29). In the Psalter it becomes an imprecation: “As a snail which melteth, let every one of them pass away: like the untimely birth of a woman, that they may not see the sun” (Psa 58:8). The ancients observed that a snail seems to consume itself as it goes, leaving a trail behind it until it is gone; the psalm asks that the wicked judges of the preceding verses — who speak wickedness, whose poison is like the poison of a serpent — may waste away in the same manner. This is one of the imprecatory psalms, and it is a prayer, not a plan: David asks God to break their teeth, and does not propose to do it. Psalm 58 ends by asserting the thing the whole psalm exists to affirm: verily he is a God that judgeth in the earth.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the snail as a slimy slow-creeping animal of the genus Helix, usually with a spiral shell; and figuratively, a drone, a slow-moving person.
webster_full: SNAIL, n. [Sax. snegel.] A slimy slow creeping animal, of the genus Helix.
The house-snail carries a spiral shell upon its back.
As a snail which melteth, let every one of them pass away. Ps. lviii.
2. A drone; a slow moving person.
scriptures: And the ferret, and the chameleon, and the lizard, and the snail, and the mole.
Psa 58:8
As a snail which melteth, let every one of them pass away: like the untimely birth of a woman, that they may not see the sun.

These also shall be unclean unto you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth; the weasel, and the mouse, and the tortoise after his kind,
corruption_summary: The imprecatory psalms are edited out of Christian use as sub-Christian, though the New Testament quotes them and the martyrs under the altar pray in their words.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 58 is one of the psalms modern hymnals and lectionaries quietly drop, on the ground that asking God to make men melt like snails cannot be prayed by people who have been told to love their enemies. Three things must be said. First, these are prayers, not programmes: the psalmist asks God to judge and does not take a weapon; the whole point is the renunciation of private vengeance in favour of the court of heaven, which is exactly what Romans commands — avenge not yourselves, for vengeance is mine, I will repay, saith the Lord. Second, the object is not personal enemies but, in this psalm, corrupt judges who oppress the poor, and the cry against them is a cry for justice. Third, the New Testament does not repudiate this register. Paul quotes Psalm 69's imprecation in Romans 11, and Revelation shows the souls under the altar crying How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood?

The right Christian use of such a psalm is neither to pray it against a neighbour who has annoyed us nor to pretend it is not in the Bible. It is to feel what it feels — a burning indignation at judges who sell the poor, at oppressors who prosper, at wickedness that has the machinery of law behind it — and to take that indignation to God rather than into one's own hands. The psalm ends where every imprecation in Scripture ends: verily he is a God that judgeth in the earth. And a Christian holds this alongside the Lord's command to pray for them that despitefully use us, because the same God who will judge the impenitent is the God who saved Saul of Tarsus while he was holding the coats.

pos: n. (a weaver of webs; in Job and Isaiah the figure of a hope and a righteousness that will not hold)
etymology: Middle English spithre, from a root meaning to spin. The Hebrew akkabish is the spider of the web passages; semamith in Proverbs 30:28 is a creature that takes hold with her hands, rendered spider and understood by some as a lizard.
biblical_def: Bildad gives the figure its classic form: “So are the paths of all that forget God; and the hypocrite's hope shall perish” (Job 8:13); “Whose hope shall be cut off, and whose trust shall be a spider's web” (Job 8:14). A web is a real structure, skilfully made and perfectly adequate for a fly; it is worthless the moment anything heavier leans on it. Isaiah applies the same picture to a nation's works: “They hatch cockatrice' eggs, and weave the spider's web: he that eateth of their eggs dieth” (Isa 59:5), and then, with terrible plainness, “Their webs shall not become garments, neither shall they cover themselves with their works: their works are works of iniquity” (Isa 59:6). Nobody has ever been clothed in a cobweb. And Proverbs sets the creature among the small and wise: “The spider taketh hold with her hands, and is in kings' palaces” (Pro 30:28), one of the “four things which are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise” (Pro 30:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the spider as an insect of the genus Aranea, remarkable for spinning webs to take its prey and for the fineness of its thread.
webster_full: SPIDER, n. The common name of the insects of the genus Aranea.
They are remarkable for spinning webs for taking their prey, and for the fineness of the thread which they draw from the body.
Whose trust shall be a spider's web. Job viii.
SPIDER-CATCHER, n. One that catches spiders.
scriptures: Job 8:14
Whose hope shall be cut off, and whose trust shall be a spider's web.
Job 8:13
So are the paths of all that forget God; and the hypocrite's hope shall perish:
Isa 59:6
Their webs shall not become garments, neither shall they cover themselves with their works: their works are works of iniquity, and the act of violence is in their hands.
The spider taketh hold with her hands, and is in kings' palaces.
corruption_summary: Sincerity is offered as the ground of acceptance with God, and Isaiah 59:6 says a man's own works will not become a garment however finely they are spun.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah's sentence is aimed precisely at self-righteousness and it grants everything except the one thing needed. The webs are real; the weaving is skilful; the workers are diligent. Their webs shall not become garments, neither shall they cover themselves with their works. The prophet had already said in an earlier chapter that all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags, and here he says the fabric will not even reach the size of a coat. That is the doctrine of justification stated negatively, and it stands against the settled assumption of nearly every religious person outside the gospel — that a sincere life, decently woven, will cover a man at the last. It will not, because the problem is not the quality of the thread but the fact that the covering must come from outside. Isaiah 61 supplies what he has denied: he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness.

Bildad's use of the figure needs a caution, since he applied it to Job and God rebuked him for the application. The proverb itself is true: a hypocrite's hope is a web, and it fails at the moment weight comes on it. What Bildad got wrong was reasoning backwards from Job's suffering to Job's hypocrisy, which is the standing error of men who hold sound principles and misapply them to their neighbours. The right use is inward. A man may test his own hope by asking what it is anchored to — whether it depends on his record, his feelings, his usefulness, or on Christ — and the test is not how the web looks in fair weather but what happens when the wind comes. Proverbs, meanwhile, lets the creature have its dignity back: little, tenacious, taking hold with her hands, and living in a king's palace.
